Always lock out and tag out all power to panels and electric components before 
servicing. 
 
 
 
 
On diesel powered systems, disconnect the battery cables to prevent damage to 
the waste reducer electrical system. 
 
 
GENERAL NOTES 
The cutter tips on the 770 waste reducers can be replaced when deemed necessary. There is no “set” way 
to tell when to replace tips. Weighing the work req uired with the machine performance is the only way to 
determine when to replace tips.  It is not necessary to replace all of the tips at the same time—only the worn 
ones need to be changed.  All of the tips should be hard-faced multiple times prior to being replaced.  This 
extends the life of the cutter tip and is much easier to do. 
 
A professional welder should do cutter tip changing.  Pre-heating and post-heating the weld area is critical to 
keep the welds from cracking as they cool.   
 
On machines with cutters welded to the shafts, this procedure must be done in the machine or with the entire 
shaft removed.  On machines with hex shafts and a stackable cutter configuration, the cutters can be removed 
from the reducer. 
 
 
CHANGING A CUTTER TIP 
1. The cutter tips are actually pairs of similar si zed tips that should be changed together.   Remove the old 
cutter tip.  Cutter tips may have been factory welded w ith either “normal” 70 series welding rod, or an 
austenitic stainless steel rod depending on the alloy of the cutter tip.  The normal rod can be scarfed 
out with a cutting torch and the stainless steel rod will have to be removed with an air arc.  The air arc 
may be the preferred tool for both types of rod since it allows the weld to be removed all the way 
down to the root.   
 
 
 
 
Be sure to ground to the object you are welding on.   If you are working on a cutter, 
ground to that cutter or elsewhere on the same cutter shaft.  If you are welding on 
the anvils or elsewhere on the cutting table, ground to the cutting table.  Serious 
damage to the bearings will result if welding current passes through them. 
 
2. Prepare the tip pocket.  The cutter tips sit in a p ocket that was burned into the cutter at the factory in 
a shape that holds the cutter tip in its location accur ately enough that no further jigs are necessary.  
After the old tip has been removed, grind away any re maining old weld material so the new tip can 
seat in the pocket fully. 
 
3. Position the new tips in place and tack weld them i n 2 or three places with ½ inch long tack welds.

4. Turn the shafts by hand to ensure that the new ti ps do not conflict with any other metal parts in the 
chamber.  If the anvils have been hard-faced, it is s ometimes necessary to grind away some hard-
facing to allow the new cutter tips to pass. 
 
5. Pre-heat the cutter and tips to at least 300°  F u sing a large “rose bud” acetylene torch.  Use a heat 
crayon to ensure that the entire area is uniformly and correctly heated.    
NOTE: This is the MOST important part of this process! 
 
6. Fully weld the cutter tips to the cutter and to each  other with at least a ½ inch deep fillet weld all 
around.  Use an austenitic stainless steel rod.  This type of rod is flexible enough to prevent cracking 
of the tip and cutter if the pre-heat is at least 300°  F. 
 
7. Post-heat the cutter and tip.  Keep the temperatu re of the cutter tip at least 250°  F for at least 1 hour 
after welding.  This can be done using a “rose bud” and insulating blankets. This step ensures that 
the welds will “normalize” to reduce weld stress, and will not develop hydrogen cracking.   
NOTE: This is the SECOND MOST important part of this process! 
 
8. After the hour of post-heating, the cutter and ti ps can be cooled to room temperature at whatever rate 
happens under insulating blankets. 
 
9. After the tips have cooled, test for adequate clea rance between the cutter and anvils again by rotating 
the shafts by hand.  If the cutters and anvils hit du ring production, there is a danger that the sparks 
will cause a fire.
